strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and relevant problem: diffusion latents are not organized for controllable traversal of dynamical processes, and the proposed editing/rendering separation (edit in a compact contrastive space C, render in the diffusion feature latent Z) is a clean, sensible design.

Evaluation spans five diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial expressions, monkey reaching), which is unusually broad for a methods paper and demonstrates generality of the pipeline.

The baseline comparison in Table 1 (same traversal operators applied in Z vs. C) is a well-conceived ablation that directly tests the claim that the contrastive space, not the operator, is what enables smooth traversal.

Reproducibility is reasonably treated: hyperparameters, architectures, training iterations, and computational resources are reported (Appendix C.1, Tables 3-5), and code/dataset release is promised under MIT license.

Limitations are candidly acknowledged (lossy embedding, local rather than global traversals, dependence on DDIM inversion), and the handling of HIPAA-protected clinical data is described appropriately.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative evidence is questionable. In Table 1, Spline in C-space achieves RMSE exactly 0.00 (and TEX-2 0.02) with PSNR/SSIM identical to TEX-2. This strongly suggests the spline is fit on the very test trajectory being 'predicted', i.e., interpolation/fitting rather than prediction, or an unclear evaluation protocol. The paper never clarifies whether the traversal operators are fit on training data and evaluated on held-out sequences, so the central claim of faithful interpolation/extrapolation is not convincingly supported.

Results are internally inconsistent and undermine confidence: for Ca2+ data, Lerp/Slerp RMSE is dramatically worse in C-space (43.87) than in Z-space (16.60) while PSNR is similar, which is not explained; TEX-1 performs worse than Lerp in Z-space despite being a superset of linear extrapolation; the text refers to 'Table 3' where the results are in a figure table on page 8.

The formal presentation is weaker than the framing suggests. Equation (4) defines the editing operator T as an argmin over a task-specific 'discrepancy loss' L and regularizer Omega that are never specified, and this formulation is never actually solved; the implemented methods (splines, finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, KDE peak interpolation) are heuristic and only loosely connected to the stated optimization.

Novelty is limited: the pipeline assembles existing components (DDIM inversion, CEBRA contrastive embeddings from neuroscience, kNN lifting, standard spline/Taylor operators). The contribution is the combination, but the paper does not isolate what is new relative to diffusion autoencoders (Preechakul et al., 2022) or geometry-preserving traversal methods (Wang and Golland, 2023; Hahm et al., 2024), which are cited as baselines but only compared via Slerp.

The kNN lift from a 3-8 dimensional embedding to the full diffusion latent Z is essentially a neighborhood-weighted lookup into training latents. It is unclear how well this generalizes to genuinely novel conditions, and the paper provides no analysis of out-of-distribution behavior, failure modes, or sensitivity to k and kernel choices (only an appendix dimension sweep).

Presentation quality is below the bar for a main-track submission: the appendix title ('Nonlinearly Controllable Counterfactuals with Diffusion') does not match the main title; a duplicated sentence appears in the monkey-reach paragraph (Section 5, Interpretability); the abstract cites 'Fig. 2' for Section 5 limitations before results are introduced; there are typos ('discrepency', 'Rsults', 'absoulte').

Quantitative evidence for the flagship claims of 'controllable generation' is thin: no generation-quality metrics (FID/IS are only used for the cLDM vs. CcGAN comparison, not for edited/traversed samples), no user study or perceptual evaluation, and improvements in classification are modest in one of two tasks (fluid: 0.78 -> 0.83 accuracy), while the TMS responder task shows only ~0.66 accuracy that may have limited practical significance.

Statistical reporting is inconsistent: standard deviations are given for PSNR/SSIM but the units/number of runs are unspecified, RMSE has no variance, and the Procrustes/RMSE improvements over PCA in the monkey task (Fig. 5) are small relative to the standard deviations reported.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem: organizing diffusion latents to support trajectory-level traversal and controllable generation, and the separation of a compact 'editing' space C from a high-fidelity 'rendering' latent space Z is a sensible architectural idea.

Evaluation spans five spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, DISFA facial expressions, TMS E-fields, monkey reach spiking), which is unusual breadth for this kind of latent-organization work, and the appendix provides unusually detailed data-acquisition documentation (e.g., FEM simulation setup, SimNIBS parameters, responder definitions).
The limitations discussion is honest in acknowledging that the embedding is lossy, favors local over global traversals, and requires DDIM inversion.

The ablation against PCA and β-VAE at matched latent dimensionality (Table 2) is a reasonable controlled comparison, and the runtime/parameter tables (Tables 4-5) support reproducibility of the computational setup.
weaknesses: The central comparative claim is not actually tested. The paper repeatedly claims superiority over 'conditioning-based baselines' (ControlNet/InstructPix2Pix-style guidance), yet no such baseline appears in any experiment. Most importantly, the cLDM itself is already conditioned on y, so direct conditional sampling at the new condition y' is an obvious, cheap baseline that is never evaluated. Without it, the claim that structured embedding + traversal beats conditioning is unsupported.

The headline trajectory results (Table 1) show near-zero RMSE (0.00-0.02) for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space, orders of magnitude better than any baseline and better than the same operators in Z. This strongly suggests circularity/leakage: a spline fit to the test trajectory trivially reproduces its own embedding points, and kNN lifting to stored training latents may be memorization rather than dynamics modeling. The evaluation protocol for 'prediction' (what is held out, how embeddings of unseen frames are obtained) is never specified clearly enough to rule this out.

The reported gains over the strongest baseline (LSTM) are small relative to error bars (e.g., fluid PSNR 35.70 ± 0.36 vs. 34.53 ± 2.05; monkey reach RMSE 1.71 ± 0.29 vs. 1.46 ± 0.45 with overlapping spread), yet the paper claims 'significant' and 'consistent' improvements throughout without any statistical testing.

Limited technical novelty. ConDA is essentially a supervised InfoNCE/CEBRA embedding (an off-the-shelf method, Schneider et al. 2023, used with the released 'offset10-model-mse' configuration) applied to DDIM-inverted latents, followed by standard B-spline fitting, finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, KDE-peak interpolation, and kNN lifting. Each component is textbook; the framing as a novel 'framework' oversells the contribution.

The method description is vague or contradictory in places: Eq. (4) defines the editing operator via an unspecified 'task-specific discrepancy loss' whose instantiation is never given; h_ψ is said to be 'intentionally lossy' while also claimed to preserve near-lossless fidelity; the kNN lifting from a 3-8 dimensional embedding back to a 32x32x4 latent space is asserted to be adequate without analysis of what information is irrecoverably lost.

Quality-control problems undermine confidence: the appendix title ('Nonlinearly Controllable Counterfactuals with Diffusion') does not match the main title; Sec. 5 references 'Table 3' where the referenced table is Figure 3's table; there are multiple typos ('a a C2-continuous', 'discrepency', 'absoulte', 'Rsults'); a placeholder '[Box link will be added]' in the reproducibility section; and Fig. 2's images are too small to support the qualitative claims about 'blurry or entangled transitions'.

The interpretability claims are thin: the monkey-reach comparison is ConDA vs. PCA only, with modest metric differences; the 'disentanglement' evidence (Appendix C.4) is a single cosine-similarity number (0.1014 vs. 0.0155) on one dataset, which is far too weak to support claims of 'successful disentanglement'.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code is 'promised' but not provided, several baselines (LSTM architecture, training data/labels for trajectory prediction, Slerp implementation) are under-specified, and the CcGAN-vs-cLDM comparison in the appendix does not connect to the main contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful problem: making pretrained diffusion latents traversable for dynamics-aware, condition-controlled generation, which prior conditioning methods (ControlNet, InstructPix2Pix) do not directly provide.

Breadth of evaluation is a real strength: five spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial expression, monkey reach spiking) with domain-appropriate datasets and reasonable split choices (blocked splits for flow, leave-subject-out for TMS).
The editing/rendering separation (compact contrastive space C for trajectory manipulation, high-fidelity latent space Z for synthesis) is a sensible and clearly articulated design.
Ablations are present: ConDA vs. PCA/β-VAE (Table 2), embedding dimensionality sweep (Fig. 13), and an orthogonality/disentanglement analysis (Table 6), plus a cLDM vs. CcGAN comparison with FID/IS.

Limitations are discussed honestly (lossy embedding, local vs. global traversals, DDIM inversion cost), and code release under MIT license is promised; clinical data handling (HIPAA protection) is addressed.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: ConDA is largely a pipeline combination of off-the-shelf components — CEBRA (used unmodified), a kNN decoder, B-splines, finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, and KDE peak interpolation. Supervised contrastive learning with auxiliary labels is well established; the contribution is applying it to DDIM-inverted diffusion latents.

A central concern is possible evaluation leakage. In Table 1, Spline and TEX-2 achieve RMSE of 0.00–0.02 and identical PSNR/SSIM in C-space — consistent with fitting the spline/Taylor model on the very sequence points being evaluated. The train/test protocol for trajectory modeling is not specified clearly enough to rule this out, and the claim of 'near-zero RMSE' as evidence of dynamics-aligned geometry is not credible without held-out sequences.

The kNN lifting decoder (Eq. 1) reconstructs Z as a weighted average of training-set latents, so reconstruction-fidelity gains may partly reflect memorization rather than learned structure; the comparison between baselines in Z and methods in C is not apples-to-apples (e.g., Spline has no Z-space entry in Table 1), confounding the headline claims.

Because the contrastive objective is supervised by the same conditions y used to condition the cLDM, the model may simply learn to encode labels rather than discover dynamics; a trivial baseline (e.g., directly embedding/regressing y, or using y as the embedding) is missing and would test whether contrastive organization is actually necessary.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: text cites 'Table 3' for SVM results but they appear in Figure 3; Table 2 numbers for the same datasets disagree with Table 1 (e.g., Ca2+ 35.69 vs. 38.58 PSNR) with no explanation of differing setups; the C-space Lerp RMSE (43.87) is worse than Z-space (16.60) and is never explained; the appendix is titled 'Nonlinearly Controllable Counterfactuals with Diffusion' while the main paper is 'ConDA', and an anonymization gap left a broken sentence ('accelerated trials at for head model reconstruction').

Counterfactual/class-transfer results (Fig. 3 right) are purely qualitative; there is no quantitative validation that interpolated responder-like E-fields match physically simulated responder fields, so the claimed clinical utility ('personalized targeting strategies') is speculative.

Missing comparisons to closely related methods the paper itself cites as motivation (e.g., diffusion autoencoders of Preechakul et al., geometry-preserving traversals of Wang and Golland/Hahm et al. are used only as Slerp), and no seed/repetition reporting for the main tables.

strengths: Broad empirical validation across five distinct spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, facial expression, TMS E-fields, monkey motor cortex), with consistent qualitative and quantitative improvements, which is unusual breadth for a latent-structuring method.

The separation of 'editing' (in a compact contrastive space C) from 'rendering' (in the diffusion latent space Z) is a clean and sensible design; the kNN lifting plus diffusion decoding preserves fidelity while allowing simple nonlinear trajectory operators (splines, Taylor extrapolation, KDE traversal) to be effective.

Good robustness/ablation evidence: solver-agnosticism is demonstrated by swapping DDIM for Rex-RK4 (8 steps) and applying the layer atop IsoDiff (Appendix C.3); kNN lifting is compared against a tuned MLP decoder (Tab. 11); embedding dimensionality is swept (Fig. 10); PCA and beta-VAE baselines are included (Tab. 4); and an orthogonality/disentanglement analysis is provided (Tab. 12).

Honest limitations section (lossy many-to-one embedding, local rather than global geometry, DDIM inversion cost), an ethics/impact statement, and detailed reproducibility material (algorithms, hyperparameters, runtimes, data access information) including a new public flow benchmark.
weaknesses: Metric circularity concerns: in Table 1, trajectory RMSE is exactly 0.00 for spline/TEX-2 in C-space across all datasets. Since the spline is fit through the observed embeddings and evaluated against those same embeddings, near-zero RMSE appears to be by construction rather than evidence of a better model; the comparison between Z-space and C-space RMSE is therefore not apples-to-apples and inflates the apparent advantage. This needs clarification or a fairer evaluation protocol.

The supervised InfoNCE objective directly organizes embeddings by the auxiliary labels (time, condition, AU intensities). Downstream wins such as better SVM classification in C-space (Tab. 3) are then close to tautological — the labels were injected during embedding training. The central claim that 'diffusion latents encode dynamics-relevant structure that ConDA exploits' would be better supported by comparisons where the label structure is not supervised in, or by quantifying how much C adds over directly using y.

The claim of outperforming 'conditioning-based baselines' (Abstract, contribution 3) is not substantiated: no quantitative comparison against directly conditioning the cLDM on the target y-trajectory is reported; the conditioning baseline comparison is limited to a cLDM-vs-CcGAN fidelity check, which is orthogonal to controllability.

Table 2 (n-step-ahead prediction) reports only ConDA C-space results with no baseline column, making the 'generalization remains stable' claim hard to assess; baselines exist only in the interpolation table.

Limited methodological novelty: the pipeline assembles off-the-shelf components (pretrained LDM VAE/UNet, DDIM/Rex-RK4 inversion, CEBRA contrastive embeddings, SciPy B-splines, kNN regression). The contribution is the combination and the editing/rendering separation, which is useful but incremental; no theoretical analysis (e.g., of when kNN lifting preserves trajectory faithfulness, or identifiability of C) is offered.

kNN lifting retrieves weighted combinations of training latents; for interpolation and counterfactual editing this risks effectively returning nearest training samples, and the paper does not measure how far generated frames deviate from training neighbors (e.g., a nearest-neighbor distance analysis or diversity metric per edit), leaving open whether 'generation' is closer to retrieval.

Some experimental details reduce confidence: embedding dimension selection via cross-validation on reconstruction scores, evaluation of only a subset of sequences per dataset (e.g., Re=120 fluid, single DISFA subject SN025 for trajectory modeling), and no error bars or seeds for many results.

strengths: The evaluation spans five genuinely diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid simulation, calcium imaging, facial expressions, TMS E-fields, monkey motor cortex), which is ambitious and gives the method broad coverage

The pipeline is clearly documented: Algorithms 1 and 2, hyperparameters (Appendix C.1), model sizes (Tab. 6), and runtimes (Tab. 7) support reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing code and the fluid benchmark dataset
The limitations section is candid and specific: lossy/many-to-one embedding, locally-biased geometry that may distort long-range traversals, and dependence on costly DDIM inversion

Robustness checks are a nice touch: the method is shown to transfer across inversion solvers (DDIM vs. Rex-RK4, Tabs. 8-10) and across diffusion models (cLDM vs. IsoDiff), and the kNN-vs-MLP lifting ablation (Tab. 11) plus dimensionality sweep (Fig. 10) probe design choices
The interpretability analysis on monkey reaching data (Fig. 5) with Procrustes distance and held-out firing-rate correlation is a reasonable attempt to go beyond pixel metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a composition of off-the-shelf components (LDM/UNet, DDIM inversion, CEBRA supervised contrastive embeddings, kNN decoder, SciPy splines, finite differences). The core idea — applying supervised contrastive learning to pretrained diffusion latents using auxiliary labels — is a straightforward application of CEBRA to a new representation source, and Eq. 2 (the editing operator) is defined only implicitly as an argmin over a vague objective with no concrete solver or guarantee

The headline near-zero RMSE values (0.00-0.02 for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space, Tab. 1) are strongly suggestive of memorization: embeddings are learned from the same sequences being interpolated, and kNN lifting reconstructs edited latents as weighted combinations of training latents. The paper does not clearly separate in-sample fits from genuine generalization for the interpolation task; held-out n-step results (RMSE 1-2) are far less impressive than the headline numbers

The kNN lifting step raises a fundamental question about what ConDA actually is: with latents lifted as weighted averages of nearby training latents, the 'generative' model borders on retrieval/interpolation of the training set, yet no experiment measures diversity, novelty, or out-of-manifold behavior of generated samples

Gains over baselines are often marginal or inconsistently reported: in Tab. 1, TEX-2 in Z-space already achieves 35.29 PSNR vs. 35.70 in C-space for fluid; several comparisons have overlapping error bars (Tab. 4 fluid RMSE: 7.47 for beta-VAE vs. 7.60 for ConDA, i.e., ConDA is worse on one metric); no statistical significance tests are reported anywhere

Baseline choices are weak or under-specified: the LSTM is trained on only 20 preceding frames, and no video diffusion, temporal S4/forecasting, or conditioning-based (ControlNet-style) baseline is evaluated on the same tasks despite the introduction criticizing conditioning methods; the GAN comparison (CcGAN) is relegated to an appendix and is not a controllability baseline

Significant presentation sloppiness suggests a recycled submission: Page 8 contains leftover ICLR 2026 submission artifacts (line numbers 1404-1457, 'Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2026', a stray 'D. REVISED RESULTS' section), Table 12 is used twice (orthogonality and revised n-step results), and metric direction arrows are inconsistent (e.g., RMSE/TAE/Procrustes marked as higher-is-better in the appendix figure/table but lower-is-better in the main text)

Classification evidence is weak: the E-Field responder F1 improves from 0.30 to 0.63, but accuracy only reaches 0.66 and AUC 0.67 with a 30/80 class split — barely above a trivial class-prior baseline; claims of 'marked improvement' overstate what these numbers support

Counterfactual/class-transfer claims (Figs. 3, 5) are validated only qualitatively or by correlation with held-out firing rates; there is no quantitative counterfactual correctness evaluation, and the KDE peak-interpolation procedure is heuristic

The abstract and introduction oversell: claims that ConDA 'transforms diffusion models into controllable generators of nonlinear spatiotemporal dynamics' are not supported given the retrieval-like lifting and interpolation-dominated evaluation

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem—organizing pretrained diffusion latents for controllable, dynamics-aware generation—and the proposed separation of editing (low-dimensional contrastive space) from rendering (diffusion latent space) is a clean and sensible design.

Unusually broad empirical coverage across five spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS E-fields, facial expressions, monkey motor cortex), including both synthetic data with ground truth and real scientific/biomedical data, with detailed dataset acquisition protocols in the appendix.

Useful ablations and robustness checks: PCA and beta-VAE representation baselines (Tab. 4), kNN vs. MLP lifting (Tab. 11), embedding-dimensionality sweeps (Fig. 10), solver-agnostic tests with Rex-RK4 and IsoDiff (Tabs. 9-10), and a disentanglement analysis via orthogonality of latent regression directions (Tab. 12).
Comparison of the underlying cLDM against CcGAN with FID/IS/reconstruction metrics (Appendix C.8) supports the choice of the diffusion backbone.

Honest, specific limitations discussion (lossy many-to-one embedding, local vs. global geometry, DDIM inversion cost) and a thoughtful impact statement addressing clinical data (HIPAA, ongoing trial) and misuse risks. Reproducibility is addressed with code release intent, hyperparameters, runtimes, and dataset access details.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the headline interpolation results: near-zero RMSE (0.00) for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space (Tab. 1) suggests the interpolator may be fit and evaluated on the same sequence frames, making the central quantitative claim (e.g., 35.7 vs. 28.3 PSNR, and Spline vs. TEX-2 differences that vanish at 0.00) difficult to interpret. The exact train/test protocol for interpolation is not clearly specified, and some reported metrics are internally odd (e.g., C-space Lerp RMSE 43.87 worse than Z-space 16.60 on Ca2+).

The motivating comparisons against conditioning-based baselines (ControlNet, InstructPix2Pix) and video diffusion models (MCVD, etc.) asserted in the introduction are never empirically evaluated; the actual baselines are only latent-space interpolation methods (Lerp/Slerp/LSTM). The claim of superiority over 'conditioning-based baselines' in the abstract is therefore not directly supported.

Limited methodological novelty: the pipeline is largely an assembly of existing components—cLDM (Rombach et al.), DDIM inversion, CEBRA supervised contrastive embeddings, SciPy B-splines/finite-difference Taylor extrapolation, and kNN-weighted latent lifting. The formal editing operator in Eq. (2) (with task-specific loss L and regularizer Omega) is never concretely instantiated or solved, making the theoretical framing looser than the actual method (splines/TEX/KDE paths).

kNN lifting reconstructs edited latents as convex combinations of training latents, which limits genuinely novel generation and calls into question claims of 'preserved diversity'; no diversity or distributional metric is reported for the editing/counterfactual tasks.

Statistical rigor is uneven: several results have zero reported variance, classification uses modest sample sizes (e.g., 30 responders vs. 80 non-responders) without confidence intervals, and Table 12 (revised results) duplicates Table 2 with inconsistent numbers and erroneous arrow directions (RMSE marked as 'higher is better').

Presentation defects: leftover review artifact on page 8 (line numbers and 'Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2026' header inconsistent with the ICML 2026 submission), typos ('discrepency', 'a a C2-continuous', 'Rsults'), and RMSE units/normalization for trajectory error are undefined.

Interpretability claims rest largely on qualitative comparisons (Figs. 3-5) and a single disentanglement statistic (cosine similarity, Tab. 12); there is no formal disentanglement or controllability metric applied consistently across the five domains.
